verifiedClaims.claim: The answer, in both Georgia and South Carolina, is yes. Your right to compensation does not disappear when the at-fault driver dies.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 ('In case of the death of the defendant, the cause of action shall survive against said defendant's personal representative'); S.C. Code § 15-5-90 (causes of action for 'injuries to the person or to personal property shall survive both to and against the personal or real representative ... of a deceased person')
verifiedClaims.note: Both survival statutes verified verbatim. SC: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t15c005.php

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia: O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 provides that causes of action for injuries to a person survive the death of either party. Your claim can be brought against the deceased driver's estate.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41: 'nor shall any action or cause of action for the recovery of damages for homicide, injury to the person, or injury to property abate by the death of either party ... In case of the death of the defendant, the cause of action shall survive against said defendant's personal representative. However, in the event of the death of the wrongdoer before an action has been brought against him, the personal representative of the wrongdoer in such capacity shall be subject to the action just as the wrongdoer himself would have been during his life, provided that there shall be no punitive damages against the personal representative.' The claim is brought against the personal representative in that capacity, and punitive damages are not available against the estate.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 (2025 Code of Georgia via Justia)
verifiedClaims.note: First sentence is right. Change 'against the deceased driver's estate' to 'against the driver's personal representative (executor or administrator)' and add the one thing the statute takes away: no punitive damages against the personal representative. Relevant on a page that mentions intoxication evidence from the autopsy.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina: S.C. Code § 15-5-90 similarly allows personal injury claims to survive the death of the tortfeasor (the person who caused the harm).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-5-90 (Survival of right of action): 'Causes of action for and in respect to ... any and all injuries to the person or to personal property shall survive both to and against the personal or real representative, as the case may be, of a deceased person'
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim match. § 15-5-100 adds that damages under § 15-5-90 may include reasonable funeral expenses.

verifiedClaims.claim: In most cases, the at-fault driver's auto liability insurance policy remains in effect even after their death. The policy covers claims arising from accidents that occurred while the driver was alive and the policy was active.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 62-3-803(d)(2) (the probate nonclaim bar places no limit on 'commencing a proceeding to establish liability of the decedent or the personal representative for which he is protected by liability insurance', 'to the limits of the insurance protection only'); O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 (personal representative 'subject to the action just as the wrongdoer himself would have been')
verifiedClaims.note: No statute says a liability policy 'remains in effect' after death; that is contract law. Both states' statutes assume it: the SC Probate Code carves insured claims out of the creditor bar, and the Georgia survival statute keeps the tort claim alive against the representative. 'In most cases' is the right hedge.

verifiedClaims.claim: The lawsuit names the estate as the defendant — for example, "Estate of John Smith, Deceased"
verifiedClaims.currentValue: In Georgia the defendant is the personal representative in his or her representative capacity, not 'the estate': 'An estate is not a legal entity which can be a party ... to legal proceedings, because the exclusive right to bring actions in behalf of an estate ... is ... in the legal representative, executor or administrator, of the estate' and a suit 'brought in a name which is neither that of a natural person, nor a corporation, nor a partnership ... is a mere nullity' (Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 119 Ga. App. 366, 166 S.E.2d 913 (1969)); O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 makes 'the personal representative of the wrongdoer in such capacity' the party subject to the action. In South Carolina 'no proceeding to enforce a claim against the estate of a decedent ... may be ... commenced before the appointment of a personal representative' (§ 62-3-104) and the proceeding is 'against the personal representative' (§ 62-3-804(2), (3)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 119 Ga. App. 366, 166 S.E.2d 913 (Ga. Ct. App. 1969); O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41; S.C. Code §§ 62-3-104, 62-3-804
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite the bullet as: the lawsuit names the personal representative of the estate as the defendant, in that capacity (for example, 'Jane Smith, as Administrator of the Estate of John Smith'). A complaint naming only 'the Estate of John Smith' can be dismissed as a nullity in Georgia.

verifiedClaims.claim: The personal representative defends the case on behalf of the estate
The deceased driver's liability insurance typically still provides the defense and pays any judgment up to policy limits
verifiedClaims.note: Same basis as the insurance-remains-in-effect claim; 'typically' is the right hedge.

verifiedClaims.claim: If the judgment exceeds policy limits, the estate's assets (bank accounts, property, investments) may be used to satisfy the remainder
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 53-7-40 (liability of estate; priority of claims); O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 (no punitive damages against the personal representative); S.C. Code § 62-3-803(a) and (d)(2) (the estate's own assets are reachable only if the claim was presented within the nonclaim period; the insurance carve-out is 'to the limits of the insurance protection only')
verifiedClaims.note: True, with two qualifications worth a clause: claims are paid in statutory priority order in Georgia, and in South Carolina the excess over insurance reaches estate assets only if the claim was timely presented in probate (see the SC creditor-deadline entry). Punitive damages never reach the estate in Georgia.

verifiedClaims.claim: Family members' personal assets are generally not at risk unless they co-signed the driver's insurance policy or were otherwise independently liable
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 'Co-signing' an insurance policy creates no liability for another person's negligence; the real independent-liability routes are the family purpose doctrine and ownership of the vehicle. South Carolina: 'a head of a family, who owns, furnishes and maintains a vehicle for the general use, pleasure and convenience of his family is liable for the negligence of a member of the family having general authority to operate the vehicle for such a purpose' (Lucht v. Youngblood, 266 S.C. 127, 221 S.E.2d 854 (S.C. 1976), a fatal-crash case against the driver's father). Georgia applies the same doctrine (Ferguson v. Gurley, 218 Ga. 276, 127 S.E.2d 462 (Ga. 1962)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Lucht v. Youngblood, 266 S.C. 127, 221 S.E.2d 854 (S.C. 1976); Ferguson v. Gurley, 218 Ga. 276, 127 S.E.2d 462 (Ga. 1962)
verifiedClaims.note: Replace 'co-signed the driver's insurance policy' with 'owned the vehicle or furnished it to the driver for family use (the family purpose doctrine), or were otherwise independently negligent'. Ferguson: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1332144/ferguson-v-gurley/

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, the probate court appoints a personal representative to manage the deceased person's estate. If the deceased had a will, the named executor petitions the court. If there was no will, the court appoints an administrator — typically a close family member.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 53-6-20 (administrator may be unanimously selected by the heirs; otherwise the probate court appoints in this order of preference: (1) the surviving spouse, (2) one or more other heirs or the person selected by a majority in interest of them, (3) any other eligible person, (4) any creditor of the estate, (5) the county administrator); O.C.G.A. § 53-6-1 (any sui juris individual is eligible regardless of residency)
verifiedClaims.note: Statutory order of preference supports 'typically a close family member'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia law, creditors (including personal injury claimants) must file their claims with the estate within a specific timeframe. Georgia requires creditors to file within the later of: (1) three months after the personal representative publishes notice to creditors, or (2) the general statute of limitations for the underlying claim.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia has no 'later of' rule and the three-month window is not a bar. O.C.G.A. § 53-7-41(b): the personal representative must, within 60 days of qualification, publish a notice to creditors once a week for four weeks; (d): creditors who fail to notify the personal representative 'within three months from the date of publication of the personal representative's last notice shall lose all rights to an equal participation with creditors of equal priority to whom distribution is made before sufficient notification of such claims is given', but 'if there are assets in the hands of the personal representative sufficient to pay such debts ... the assets shall be thus appropriated notwithstanding the failure of such creditors to notify the personal representative of their claims in a timely manner.' Separately, § 53-7-42(b): 'No action to recover a debt due by the decedent shall be commenced against the personal representative until the expiration of six months from the date of qualification of the first personal representative to serve.' The two-year tort limitation (§ 9-3-33) still governs, and § 9-3-93 tolls it for creditors while the estate is unrepresented: 'The time between the death of a person and the commencement of representation upon his estate ... shall not be counted against creditors of his estate, provided that such time does not exceed five years'; § 9-3-98 makes that article apply 'to tort actions as well as actions on contracts'.
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite the paragraph: give the personal representative written notice of the claim within three months of the last published notice so the claim shares in distributions; no suit may be filed against the personal representative for six months after qualification (§ 53-7-42(b)); the two-year limitation period is paused, up to five years, while no personal representative is in place (§ 9-3-93). § 53-7-42: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-53/chapter-7/article-4/section-53-7-42/ ; § 9-3-93: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-9/chapter-3/article-5/section-9-3-93/

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina requires that claims be filed within one year from the date of the decedent's death or within the applicable statute of limitations, whichever is earlier.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 62-3-803(a): claims that arose before death, 'founded on contract, tort, or other legal basis', are barred against the estate, the personal representative, heirs, devisees and nonprobate transferees 'unless presented within the earlier of the following: (1) one year after the decedent's death; or (2) the time provided by Section 62-3-801(b) for creditors who are given actual notice, and within the time provided in Section 62-3-801(a) for all creditors barred by publication.' § 62-3-801(a): the published notice requires creditors 'to present their claims within eight months after the date of the first publication of the notice or be forever barred'; (b): written notice to a known creditor sets the earlier of one year from death or sixty days from mailing. The 'whichever is earlier' comparison is to the eight-month publication period (or sixty-day actual-notice period), not to the statute of limitations. Two more rules the post omits: § 62-3-803(d)(2) exempts from the bar, 'to the limits of the insurance protection only, commencing a proceeding to establish liability of the decedent or the personal representative for which he is protected by liability insurance'; and § 62-3-802(b) suspends the running of the ordinary statute of limitations 'during the eight months following the decedent's death'.
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential correction in the post. As written it tells a South Carolina reader whose claim is within the driver's insurance limits that the claim dies one year after the driver's death; the Probate Code says the opposite. Rewrite: to reach the estate's own assets, present the claim in probate (§ 62-3-804) within the earlier of one year after death or eight months after the first published notice to creditors (sixty days after any written notice); a claim covered by the driver's liability insurance is not subject to that bar up to the policy limits, and the three-year limitation period is paused for eight months after the death.

verifiedClaims.claim: In both states, if the estate has not yet been opened (no one has petitioned the court to begin the probate process), your attorney may need to petition the court to appoint a personal representative so that you have a party to sue. This is a procedural step, but it can add time to the process.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 53-6-20 (order of preference for appointment of an administrator includes '(4) Any creditor of the estate'); S.C. Code § 62-3-203(a)(6) (priority for appointment: 'forty-five days after the death of the decedent, any creditor complying with the requirements of Section 62-3-804(1)(b)'); § 62-3-804(1)(b) (creditor seeking appointment attaches the written statement of claim, which counts as presentation); § 62-3-104 (no proceeding against the estate before a personal representative is appointed)
verifiedClaims.note: Verified in both states; the claimant is a creditor with standing to seek appointment. Optional precision: in South Carolina the creditor may apply 45 days after death, and in Georgia the limitation period is tolled while the estate is unrepresented (§ 9-3-93).

verifiedClaims.claim: UM/UIM required? | Offered but can be rejected in writing (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(1), (a)(3) (coverage 'shall not be applicable where any insured named in the policy shall reject the coverage in writing')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1757 (verified 2026-09-23).

verifiedClaims.claim: UM is mandatory in every policy and cannot be rejected (S.C. Code § 38-77-150); UIM must be offered but is optional (S.C. Code § 38-77-160)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150(A), 38-77-160; Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co. v. Erwood (S.C. 2007)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1757; matches the writer-profile table (UM mandatory, § 38-77-150).

verifiedClaims.claim: Stacking allowed? | Yes, unless waived | Yes, unless waived
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Neither state has an 'anti-stacking waiver'. Georgia: UM coverage from separate policies stacks and policy clauses preventing that are unenforceable (State Farm v. Hancock, 164 Ga. App. 32 (1982)); vehicles on a single policy generally do not stack (Crafter v. State Farm, 251 Ga. App. 642 (2001)). South Carolina: only a Class I insured (named insured or resident relative with a vehicle involved in the crash) may stack, capped at the coverage on the vehicle involved, and exclusions blocking that are invalid (S.C. Code § 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Ins. Co., 406 S.C. 609 (2013)); a Class II insured cannot stack.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Crafter v. State Farm Ins. Co. (Ga. Ct. App. 2001); State Farm v. Hancock (Ga. Ct. App. 1982); S.C. Code § 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Ins. Co. (S.C. 2013)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-1757. Change both cells to 'Yes, with limits (separate policies in Georgia; Class I insureds in South Carolina)' and drop 'unless waived'. Carter: https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/2013/27340.html

verifiedClaims.claim: Covers deceased uninsured driver? | Yes | Yes
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(b)(1)(D) (an 'uninsured motor vehicle' is defined by the absence or insufficiency of liability coverage on the vehicle, not by the driver's survival) and (d) (the UM carrier is served with the tort action against the known owner or operator 'as though the insurance company were actually named as a party defendant'); S.C. Code § 38-77-30(14)-(15) (definitions of uninsured and underinsured motor vehicle); §§ 38-77-150(B), 38-77-160 (UM/UIM carrier served with the liability action)
verifiedClaims.note: Nothing in either UM statute turns on whether the at-fault driver lived. Mechanics when the driver died: the tort action is brought against the driver's personal representative and the UM/UIM carrier is served as a party in interest (Georgia § 33-7-11(d); South Carolina §§ 38-77-150(B), 38-77-160). Worth one sentence in the UM section.

verifiedClaims.claim: Who can file | Surviving spouse; if none, children; if none, parents (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 51-4-2(a) covers the spouse and children only: 'The surviving spouse or, if there is no surviving spouse, a child or children, either minor or sui juris, may recover for the homicide of the spouse or parent the full value of the life of the decedent.' The parents' right is a separate section, § 51-4-4 ('The right to recover for the homicide of a child shall be as provided in Code Section 19-7-1 and Code Section 53-1-5'), and if no one qualifies under § 51-4-2 or § 51-4-4 'the administrator or executor of the decedent may bring an action' for the next of kin (§ 51-4-5(a)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. §§ 51-4-2(a), 51-4-4, 51-4-5(a) (2025 Code of Georgia via Justia)
verifiedClaims.note: Order is right; the cite is over-broad. Change to 'Surviving spouse; if none, children (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2); if none, parents (§ 51-4-4); otherwise the estate's administrator or executor (§ 51-4-5)'. § 51-4-4: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-51/chapter-4/section-51-4-4/ ; § 51-4-5: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-51/chapter-4/section-51-4-5/

verifiedClaims.claim: Who can file | Personal representative of the estate (S.C. Code § 15-51-20)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-51-20: 'Every such action shall be brought by or in the name of the executor or administrator of such person.'
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim; matches the writer-profile table and SC.json authority 'SC 15-51-20'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Statute of limitations | 2 years from date of death (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 ('actions for injuries to the person shall be brought within two years after the right of action accrues'); GA.json rule wrongful-death-deadline-cited-to-definitions ('The two-year wrongful death deadline is § 9-3-33')
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-2647 and facts-1757.

verifiedClaims.claim: Statute of limitations | 3 years from date of death (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-3-530(6): 'an action under Sections 15-51-10 to 15-51-60 for death by wrongful act, the period to begin to run upon the death of the person on account of whose death the action is brought'
verifiedClaims.note: Subsection (6) verified verbatim; accrual at death is in the statute.

verifiedClaims.claim: Damages recovered for | "Full value of the life" of the deceased
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-4-2(a) ('the full value of the life of the decedent, as shown by the evidence'); § 51-4-5(a)

verifiedClaims.claim: Damages recovered for | Pecuniary loss to beneficiaries + punitive damages
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina wrongful-death damages are not limited to pecuniary loss. S.C. Code § 15-51-40: 'the jury may give damages, including exemplary damages when the wrongful act, neglect, or default was the result of recklessness, wilfulness, or malice, as they may think proportioned to the injury resulting from the death to the parties respectively for whom and for whose benefit such action shall be brought.' The Supreme Court: 'Mental shock and suffering, wounded feelings, grief, sorrow, and loss of society and companionship are recoverable in a wrongful death action' (Garner v. Houck, 312 S.C. 481, 435 S.E.2d 847 (S.C. 1993), citing Smith v. Wells, 258 S.C. 316, 188 S.E.2d 470 (S.C. 1972)). Exemplary damages are subject to the § 15-32-530 cap (greater of three times compensatory or $500,000) and, against a deceased driver's estate, are a practical question the post should not promise.
verifiedClaims.note: Change the cell to 'Pecuniary loss plus mental shock, grief and loss of companionship of the beneficiaries; exemplary damages for reckless or wilful conduct (S.C. Code § 15-51-40)'. Garner: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1225184/garner-ex-rel-estate-of-garner-v-houck/

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia personal injury: 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33)
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table. When the driver died, § 9-3-93 tolls this period (up to five years) while the estate has no personal representative; worth a sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina personal injury: 3 years from the date of the accident (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table. § 62-3-802(b) suspends the period for eight months after the driver's death.

verifiedClaims.claim: Probate creditor deadlines may impose additional requirements — particularly in South Carolina, where claims against the estate must be filed within one year of death
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina: the earlier of one year after death or eight months after the first published notice to creditors (§§ 62-3-801(a), 62-3-803(a)), and the bar does not apply, up to the policy limits, to a claim covered by the decedent's liability insurance (§ 62-3-803(d)(2)). Georgia: written notice to the personal representative within three months of the last published notice preserves equal participation in distributions (§ 53-7-41(d)); no suit against the personal representative for six months after qualification (§ 53-7-42(b)).
verifiedClaims.note: Same correction as the South Carolina Probate paragraph; this bullet repeats the one-year error.

verifiedClaims.claim: The interaction between the personal injury statute of limitations and the probate creditor deadline can create a compressed timeline. If the at-fault driver died in the accident, you may need to act quickly to ensure your claim is filed properly in both the civil court and the probate proceeding. Do not assume you have the full two or three years — consult an attorney as soon as possible.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The compression is real only for the part of a claim that exceeds the driver's liability insurance and must reach estate assets. For the insured part, both states loosen rather than tighten the clock: Georgia tolls the two-year period for up to five years while the estate is unrepresented (§ 9-3-93, applied to torts by § 9-3-98) and bars suit for the first six months after a personal representative qualifies (§ 53-7-42(b)); South Carolina suspends the three-year period for eight months after death (§ 62-3-802(b)) and exempts insured claims from the nonclaim bar to the policy limits (§ 62-3-803(d)(2)). 'Act quickly' remains sound advice for preserving the excess claim and for evidence.
verifiedClaims.note: Keep the urgency, fix the mechanism: the probate deadline threatens the uninsured excess, not the whole claim, and the ordinary limitation period is paused, not shortened, by the driver's death.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-5-90) both allow personal injury claims to survive the tortfeasor's death.
You can pursue the claim through the driver's liability insurance, a lawsuit against their estate, or your own UM/UIM coverage.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Against their estate' is acceptable shorthand in the takeaways; the body should name the personal representative.

verifiedClaims.claim: Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia and three in South Carolina, but probate creditor deadlines may compress the timeline further.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530); the driver's death pauses those clocks (Georgia § 9-3-93; South Carolina § 62-3-802(b)), but any recovery beyond the driver's insurance must also be presented as a probate claim, in South Carolina within the earlier of one year after death or eight months after notice to creditors (§ 62-3-803).
verifiedClaims.note: The Key Takeaways box renders above the article; the current sentence implies the whole claim is compressed.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. In both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-5-90), personal injury claims survive the death of the at-fault party. You can pursue compensation through the deceased driver's liability insurance, a lawsuit against their estate, or your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.
verifiedClaims.note: Renders into FAQPage structured data; accurate as written.

verifiedClaims.claim: No. You sue the deceased driver's estate, not the family members personally. The estate is a legal entity managed by a personal representative (executor) appointed by the probate court. The deceased driver's liability insurance typically defends the case and pays any judgment up to policy limits. Family members' personal assets are generally not at risk.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No. You sue the personal representative of the deceased driver's estate (the executor or administrator appointed by the probate court) in that capacity, not the family members personally; in Georgia an 'estate' is not itself a legal entity that can be sued (Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 119 Ga. App. 366 (1969); O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41), and in South Carolina the proceeding is against the personal representative (S.C. Code § 62-3-804). The driver's liability insurance typically defends and pays up to the policy limits. Family members' own assets are generally not at risk unless they owned or furnished the vehicle (family purpose doctrine) or were independently negligent.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky (Ga. Ct. App. 1969); O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41; S.C. Code § 62-3-804; Lucht v. Youngblood (S.C. 1976)
verifiedClaims.note: 'The estate is a legal entity' is the reverse of Georgia law. Renders into FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: If the deceased driver was uninsured or underinsured, you may file a claim through your own uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage. You may also pursue a claim against the estate's assets through probate court. An attorney can identify all available sources of recovery to maximize your compensation.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: UM/UIM part is correct (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11; S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150, 38-77-160). The estate part needs the mechanism: in South Carolina the claim is presented in the probate court and then sued on against the personal representative in any court with jurisdiction (§ 62-3-804(2)-(3)), within the § 62-3-803 deadline; in Georgia the claim is noticed to the personal representative (§ 53-7-41) and the tort suit is filed against the personal representative after the six-month waiting period (§ 53-7-42(b)). The probate court does not itself try the injury claim.
verifiedClaims.note: Change 'pursue a claim against the estate's assets through probate court' to 'present a claim in the probate proceeding and sue the personal representative'. Renders into FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: The standard statutes of limitations apply — two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). However, probate creditor deadlines may impose additional requirements, particularly in South Carolina where claims against the estate must be filed within one year of death. Consult an attorney promptly to avoid missing any deadlines.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), and the driver's death pauses those periods (Georgia: while the estate has no personal representative, up to five years, § 9-3-93; South Carolina: eight months after death, § 62-3-802(b)). To reach the estate's own assets beyond the insurance, present a probate claim: in South Carolina within the earlier of one year after death or eight months after the first published notice to creditors (§ 62-3-803(a)), a bar that does not apply to the insured part of the claim (§ 62-3-803(d)(2)); in Georgia notify the personal representative within three months of the last published notice (§ 53-7-41(d)).
verifiedClaims.note: The one-year statement is repeated here and in the FAQPage structured data; fix all three surfaces (body probate paragraph, deadlines bullet, this FAQ) together.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your claim is primarily against the insurance company, not the deceased driver's family. Auto insurance exists for this exact purpose — the at-fault driver paid premiums so their insurer would cover damages from their negligence. Your medical bills, lost wages, and suffering are real regardless of the other driver's fate, and not pursuing the claim only leaves you bearing the full financial burden.
verifiedClaims.note: No statute or figure asserted; consistent with the verified insurance carve-out.

verifiedClaims.claim: The deceased driver cannot testify, which means the insurance company may try to shift blame onto you without contradiction. This makes objective evidence critical: police reports, witness statements, dashcam footage, accident reconstruction analysis, cell phone records, and toxicology reports from the autopsy can all help establish fault in the absence of the other driver's testimony.
verifiedClaims.note: Evidentiary generality; nothing to verify.

verifiedClaims.claim: Your claim survives the at-fault driver's death. How to pursue it in Georgia or South Carolina through insurance, the estate, or your own coverage.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as the Article description; accurate.

recommendedEdits: Survival bullets: change 'Your claim can be brought against the deceased driver's estate' to 'against the driver's personal representative (executor or administrator)' and add that O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 bars punitive damages against the personal representative.

Suing the Estate bullets: replace 'The lawsuit names the estate as the defendant — for example, "Estate of John Smith, Deceased"' with 'The lawsuit names the personal representative, in that capacity, as the defendant (for example, "Jane Smith, as Administrator of the Estate of John Smith"); in Georgia an estate is not a legal entity that can be sued (Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 1969).'

Suing the Estate bullets: replace 'unless they co-signed the driver's insurance policy' with 'unless they owned or furnished the vehicle for family use (the family purpose doctrine) or were otherwise independently negligent'.

Georgia Probate paragraph: delete the 'later of ... three months ... or the general statute of limitations' sentence; state instead that the personal representative publishes notice within 60 days of qualifying (O.C.G.A. § 53-7-41(b)), that written notice of the claim within three months of the last publication preserves equal participation in distributions but does not bar the claim (§ 53-7-41(d)), that no suit may be filed against the personal representative for six months after qualification (§ 53-7-42(b)), and that the two-year period is tolled up to five years while the estate has no personal representative (§ 9-3-93, applied to torts by § 9-3-98).

South Carolina Probate paragraph: replace 'within one year from the date of the decedent's death or within the applicable statute of limitations, whichever is earlier' with 'within the earlier of one year after the death or eight months after the first published notice to creditors (sixty days after any written notice), S.C. Code §§ 62-3-801, 62-3-803(a)'; add that this bar does not apply, up to the policy limits, to a claim covered by the driver's liability insurance (§ 62-3-803(d)(2)), and that the three-year limitation period is suspended for eight months after death (§ 62-3-802(b)).

Both-states probate sentence: optionally add that a claimant is a creditor who may seek appointment (Georgia § 53-6-20(4); South Carolina § 62-3-203(a)(6), 45 days after death, attaching the statement of claim under § 62-3-804(1)(b)).

UM/UIM table 'Stacking allowed?' row: change both cells from 'Yes, unless waived' to 'Yes, with limits' (Georgia: separate policies stack, vehicles on one policy do not; South Carolina: Class I insureds only, capped at the coverage on the vehicle involved); no waiver exists in either state.

UM/UIM section: add one sentence that when the at-fault driver died the tort action is brought against the personal representative and the UM/UIM carrier is served as a party in interest (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(d); S.C. Code §§ 38-77-150(B), 38-77-160).
Wrongful death table 'Who can file' (Georgia): cite the parents' right to § 51-4-4 and the fallback to the administrator or executor to § 51-4-5; keep § 51-4-2 for spouse and children only.

Wrongful death table 'Damages recovered for' (South Carolina): replace 'Pecuniary loss to beneficiaries + punitive damages' with 'Pecuniary loss plus the beneficiaries' mental shock, grief and loss of companionship; exemplary damages for reckless or wilful conduct (S.C. Code § 15-51-40; Garner v. Houck, 1993)'.

Filing Deadlines section: rewrite the probate bullet and the 'compressed timeline' paragraph so the compression applies to recovery beyond the insurance limits, and say that the driver's death pauses the ordinary limitation period (Georgia § 9-3-93; South Carolina § 62-3-802(b)).
Comparative fault: optionally attribute the South Carolina 51 percent rule to Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (1991); never cite § 15-38-15.

Key takeaways: rewrite the deadlines sentence per the Filing Deadlines correction (death pauses the clock; probate deadline governs recovery beyond the insurance; South Carolina earlier of one year or eight months after notice).

faq:1: replace 'The estate is a legal entity managed by a personal representative (executor)' with 'You sue the personal representative (executor or administrator) in that capacity'; add the family purpose qualifier.
faq:2: change 'pursue a claim against the estate's assets through probate court' to 'present a claim in the probate proceeding and sue the personal representative'.

faq:3: replace the 'within one year of death' sentence with the corrected South Carolina rule (earlier of one year or eight months after published notice; insured claims exempt to the policy limits) and the Georgia three-month notice, and add that the driver's death pauses the limitation periods.

caseCitations.name: Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 119 Ga. App. 366, 166 S.E.2d 913 (Ga. Ct. App. 1969)
caseCitations.holding: An estate is not a legal entity that can be a party to legal proceedings; the right to sue or be sued is in the executor or administrator, and a suit in the name of a non-entity is a nullity.

caseCitations.name: Lucht v. Youngblood, 266 S.C. 127, 221 S.E.2d 854 (S.C. 1976)
caseCitations.holding: Family purpose doctrine: a head of family who owns, furnishes and maintains a vehicle for general family use is liable for the negligence of a family member driving it with general authority.

caseCitations.name: Ferguson v. Gurley, 218 Ga. 276, 127 S.E.2d 462 (Ga. 1962)
caseCitations.holding: Georgia Supreme Court applying the family purpose doctrine to a vehicle owner for a family member's negligent driving.

caseCitations.name: Garner v. Houck, 312 S.C. 481, 435 S.E.2d 847 (S.C. 1993)
caseCitations.holding: Mental shock and suffering, wounded feelings, grief, sorrow, and loss of society and companionship are recoverable in a South Carolina wrongful death action (citing Smith v. Wells, 258 S.C. 316 (1972)).

caseCitations.name: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (S.C. 1991)
caseCitations.holding: South Carolina modified comparative negligence: plaintiff recovers if their negligence is not greater than the defendant's.

caseCitations.name: Crafter v. State Farm Ins. Co., 251 Ga. App. 642, 554 S.E.2d 571 (Ga. Ct. App. 2001)
caseCitations.holding: Georgia UM benefits stack across available policies; no stacking within a single policy covering several vehicles.

caseCitations.name: Carter v. Standard Fire Ins. Co., 406 S.C. 609, 753 S.E.2d 515 (S.C. 2013)
caseCitations.holding: Class I insured with UIM on the involved vehicle may stack UIM on at-home vehicles; contrary exclusion invalid under § 38-77-160.
